set.st: Frank G. Stocking (Morgan Hill, Cal., 1914), whose family knew Wabasis, wrote that the chief's oldest daughter told his grandmother the money (silver, in a copper kettle covered with moss) was taken by canoe up the creek and buried. He hunted it and left a pick and shovel there about 1879. The 1922 nephew account says gold in a tin pail inside an iron kettle. In January 1889 a state-news wire said two Rockford men thought they knew where the fortune lay and were digging for it; no outcome was reported. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself. A 1922 family account adds that the chief later moved the kettle of silver by canoe 'up the creek'; nobody knew where. Spot from Stocking's 1914 directions: 1/2 to 3/4 mile up Wabasis Creek from the Little Wabasis outlet, about 10 rods off the creek. Creek course from the 1972 USGS topo, so it may have shifted since the 1870s. About 1918 a party from New York came to Belding claiming to know the spot, then suddenly packed up and left; many locals believed they got it (unconfirmed). The 1880 telling (earliest print found): the chief received about $10,000 at Grand Rapids for tribal lands, put it in a strong box and sank it in Wahnoketo (Wabasis) Lake; he was killed for it and his bones later found on the shore; 'no trace of the treasure'. The paper's sequel of a man digging up an oak coffer of gold is a comic tall tale, not a find. Jud W. King's 1922 defence of the chief gives the nephew's account in full: about 1890 the old Methodist preacher near Kiddville told King the treaty gold filled an eight-quart tin pail to within 2½ inches of the top, set inside a covered iron kettle; after the eloping daughter took some, Wabasis dug it up to show the tribe, then he and his crippled son reburied it in a new place; Wabasis was stabbed pursuing the couple and the son died soon after without telling. A 1921 Lakeview Enterprise piece has him burying it 'somewhere along the shores of the lake he loved' (per his rival Neoggamah), with the shores 'dug up in various places, yet no trace'. The Belding Banner (4 Oct 1916) says Barney Race and Ed Whitford probed the shore of Little Wabasis Lake for the kettle; the 1922 Stocking letter names the Olsgaard farm north of Belding as the family place.

src: Livingston County Press-Argus and Oakland County Advertiser, 10 Jan 1889 (state-news wire; Newspapers.com 453064240)
